extracted.intended_audience: legislators, government policymakers, administrative agencies, parliamentary committees, and administrative law practitioners
extracted.subtask_short: agency policy and parliamentary review standards
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and recommended procedures for (1) when and how executive policy directions may be issued to independent administrative agencies, (2) the formulation, publication and legal character of agency policy statements (non‑binding and binding), and (3) parliamentary and executive review mechanisms for agencies. Focus is on structuring discretion, transparency, consultation, and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority for short-term 'freeze orders' but not 'stop orders'
rubrics_metrics.description: Favours authority to issue ninety-day 'freeze orders' to preclude the agency from processing new applications pending development and announcement of government policy on an anticipated issue; does not endorse 'stop orders' to halt a proceeding already under way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freeze orders can temporarily pause intake while policy is developed; stop orders that halt active proceedings are disfavoured as they interfere with specific cases (cites change from Working Paper 25).

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy directions as statutory instruments subject to publication and parliamentary scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Directions should be subject to the Statutory Instruments Act so that they are published in the Canada Gazette and tabled in Parliament and subject to scrutiny by the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making directions statutory instruments ensures openness and parliamentary oversight (example: Salco Footwear treating a ministerial direction as a statutory instrument).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies may initiate political-direction processes but normal policy development should be agency-led
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies would be able to initiate the process for political direction, much as they do today when they wish the Government to make a regulation, but normal policy development should still be spearheaded by the agencies themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may seek political clout in exceptional circumstances, but routine policy elaboration should remain agency-driven; this preserves agency expertise and responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only Governor in Council should have authority to issue binding policy directions (not individual ministers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where statutory authority is needed to allow the executive to issue binding policy directions, it is the Governor in Council who should be empowered to do so; individual ministers should not have that authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two reasons given: policy directions should reflect broad governmental policy not single-department perspectives; ministers may be conflicted between their department and an agency and need Cabinet as a buffer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies must interpret and apply policy directions as formal legislative instruments; cannot routinely refer them back to Cabinet for interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: A policy direction is a formal legislative instrument; the agency should interpret and apply that instrument, as it would any other law, until it is replaced by the authority that issued it or definitively interpreted by the courts; agencies should not refer directions back to Cabinet for interpretation or clarification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This treats directions like regulations/statutes and discourages agencies from shifting interpretive burdens to Cabinet; it also prevents Cabinet from extending policy to new situations without following regulation-making processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy directions should be issued sparingly and not to exert direct control over adjudicative functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Not endorsing general use of policy directions; their potential negative impact upon the administrative process is of concern; they are inappropriate to exert direct control over agency decisions, especially specialized adjudicative functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directions should minimize interference with roles Parliament has given agencies; sparing use helps preserve agency legitimacy and responsibility (cites LRCC, Rec. 4.6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy directions should be issued only after appropriate consultation with a public record
rubrics_metrics.description: Directions should only be issued after an appropriate measure of consultation, particularly where they would effect a substantial policy change; the forum for consultation should be flexible and may include the agency, department, parliamentary committee, royal commission or other inquiry; in all cases there should be a public record of views of those participating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consultation should allow interested persons to influence government policy; the agency's comments and expertise should be sought and recorded; prior practice rarely gave interested persons an opportunity to influence policy directions (example: CRTC directions lacked formal consultation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies should make advance statements of policy (to structure and communicate decision criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should be encouraged to work, formally and informally, at structuring and communicating the criteria upon which they base their decisions and to make policy statements as early as possible so those who deal with the agency can anticipate how discretion will be exercised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy statements separate generic policy considerations from particularized case considerations; examples include Revenue Canada interpretation bulletins, Canadian Pension Commission guidelines, CRTC public notices; 'generic hearings' could be held to acquire input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative encouragement for non‑binding policy statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament should confer on independent administrative agencies, as an express statutory power, the authority to formulate non-binding policy statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court accepts policy statements as permissible and 'eminently proper' provided agencies do not treat them as binding or fetter discretion (cases: Capital Cities, Maple Lodge Farms). Agencies need no legislative authority to adopt them, but statutory encouragement would be beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to issue binding policy statements to structure discretion where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should be authorized to issue binding policy statements to structure, in a definitive way, areas of discretion left to the agency by Parliament; working criteria in non-binding statements may crystallize into binding ones where the agency has a firm view of what ought in all cases to condition exercise of its discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Binding policy statements eliminate needless repetitive argument in individual cases and provide certainty and equal treatment; may be necessary when enabling legislation limits Charter rights (example: censoring authority) to ensure the limitation is 'prescribed by law' under s.1 of the Charter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binding policy statements should be open to scrutiny and participation but with flexible processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Because binding policy statements represent a special manner of exercising discretion, their scrutiny and participation processes should be flexible so as not to discourage agencies from undertaking this authority; for example, they should be subject to notice-and-comment procedures but exempted from preliminary screening requirements of the Statutory Instruments Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow agencies to experiment and avoid overformalizing the process early on; processes used for regulation-making may be useful but must balance openness with practical flexibility; agencies should be able to test approaches without being deterred by excessive formalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binding policy statements should be published, maintained accessibly, and subject to parliamentary oversight and disallowance
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should be required to maintain all policy statements, binding or not, in an accessible format and to publish them when made; binding policy statements should also stand referred to the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments and be subject to disallowance by Parliament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication and referral promote transparency and parliamentary control similar to other subordinate legislation; helps public measure agency policy against recorded views from consultations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binding policy statements should not impose obligations on private persons; they condition agency discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Since these statements cover areas of discretion in decision making, they would not create obligations on private persons; rather, they would condition the agency's area of discretion and bind the agency by conditions or entitlements until changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This avoids imposing liability for breach on private parties and frames binding statements as internal constraints on the agency's conduct, benefiting those who deal with the agency through certainty and discouraging repetitious applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies should separate policy-level considerations from individual adjudicative considerations and consider alternative procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should consider developing policy-statements about how they will exercise discretion before being required to do so in a specific application, and should separate policy considerations relating to a range of applications from particularized considerations applying to individual situations; 'generic hearings' could acquire necessary input.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including many interests in a proceeding can make it complex and costly; procedural rights appropriate for aggrieved persons may be inappropriate for those only concerned with broad policy; separating processes can improve efficiency and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefits expected from policy statements: voluntary compliance, consistency, accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy statements can facilitate voluntary compliance, ensure greater consistency in decision making and encourage accountability; agencies and the public gain certainty and a greater sense of equal treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While helpful, the importance of structuring discretion must not be overestimated; policy statements are tools to improve administration and should be used prudently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary committees should have a clear mandate and capacity to scrutinize agencies and their reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Standing committees should play a more direct role, have a clear mandate to scrutinize the activities of particular agencies, and exert influence over the shape and content of agency reports to ensure they provide the information necessary to understand the agency's role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annual reports should identify the mandate and objectives, explain how they are interpreted, outline agency philosophy and plans, describe major activities and how they helped achieve goals; committees should receive agency reports automatically is insufficient—active engagement is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary scrutiny requires expertise, continuity, and resources (moderate secretariat)
rubrics_metrics.description: To make adequate evaluations, committees must acquire understanding of relevant legislation, regulations and policy statements and their practical implications; smaller committees with continuity of membership and a moderate secretariat should be provided to help focus on key issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation entails time, research and study; parliamentary members need resources that have not traditionally been provided; without these, reforms like sunsets risk undermining agency independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer efficient use of existing parliamentary mechanisms over sunset provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: There is doubt about the need to introduce sunset provisions; existing mechanisms (estimates, discussion of annual reports, other tools) could be explored to carry out agency evaluation; parliamentary attitude is more crucial than procedural form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sunset provisions are difficult to manage and may compromise agency independence if parliamentary committee systems are weak; fine tuning and using traditional mechanisms may be more effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political appeals are distinct from judicial appeals and are problematic in practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Political appeals (statutory right to apply to Cabinet or a minister to review an agency decision) raise policy questions not questions of fact or law; they generally lack procedural requirements, are secretive, susceptible to extraneous influences, and may reverse agency determinations on irrelevant 'evidence'. They are particularly inappropriate where agencies were established to be insulated from mainstream politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political appeals can demoralize agencies and parties, undermine credibility, and permit reversals motivated by partisan purposes; their processes and appropriateness should be re-examined because they do not adequately provide merits review or proper governmental oversight.
